title: Electric Powertrain: Vertical Aerospace Expands in Bristol
html:
As electric aviation moves closer to commercial production, developing reliable batteries and propulsion systems remains one of the industry’s biggest engineering challenges. Vertical Aerospace has completed construction of a new 30,000-square-foot Powertrain Centre in Bristol, UK, to support the certification and early production of its electric aircraft.

The facility will bring battery manufacturing, power electronics, propulsion integration, and testing under one roof. Equipment installation and engineering work will follow, with operations expected to ramp up in 2027.

For eeNews Europe readers, the expansion is particularly relevant to advances in battery technology, power electronics, and electric propulsion. It also shows how aerospace manufacturers are preparing to scale these technologies while meeting the demanding safety and certification requirements of aviation.

Expanding Electric Powertrain Development

Located beside Vertical’s existing Energy Centre, the new Powertrain Centre will support both the all-electric Valo aircraft and the company’s hybrid-electric program.

The facility is expected to triple Vertical’s battery-production capacity over time, helping the company manufacture packs for certification aircraft and its first commercial customers.

Its engineering activities will focus on integrating batteries, power electronics, and propulsion systems, allowing the company to test how these components perform together.

“This centre will bring together batteries, power electronics and propulsion systems for integrated development and testing, while scaling battery production for certification aircraft and our first customers,” said Richard Moore, VP of Powertrain at Vertical Aerospace.

The new facility builds on the 15,000-square-foot Vertical Energy Centre, which opened in 2023 and has produced batteries for the company’s piloted flight tests since 2024.

Battery Production Beyond Aircraft Delivery

Vertical also sees battery production as a long-term business opportunity.

The company expects each aircraft to require approximately 20 battery packs over its operational lifetime, creating demand for replacement batteries beyond the initial aircraft sale.

The new center will also develop battery recycling, reuse, and remanufacturing capabilities. These could eventually support second-life applications in aerospace, high-power charging, and other mobility sectors.

Managing battery performance throughout an aircraft’s service life is particularly important for electric aviation, where energy storage directly affects range, payload, and operating costs.

Preparing for Certification and Early Production

Vertical has already produced its first all-electric Valo battery using an upgraded assembly line at its existing Energy Centre.

The company has also begun testing its next-generation hybrid-electric propulsion system on a dedicated Hybrid Propulsion Evaluation Rig, known as HYPER, at Cotswold Airport.

The Bristol facilities will work alongside Vertical’s Aircraft Assembly Centre, which opened at Cotswold Airport in September 2026.

Together, these sites will support engineering, battery manufacturing, aircraft assembly, and the preparation of certification aircraft.

Vertical is also expected to announce the location of its first full-scale aircraft production facility before the end of 2026.

The company’s four-passenger Valo aircraft is designed for electric vertical takeoff and landing, while a hybrid-electric variant is being developed to offer greater range and operational flexibility.

With construction of the Powertrain Centre complete, the next challenge will be translating these engineering capabilities into certified aircraft and repeatable production processes.
